Since the early 2020s, a large share of office employees has worked from home for at least part of the week, and the question of how this affects productivity has produced a surprising range of answers. Studies based on self-reported data tend to find that employees feel more productive at home, mainly because they avoid commuting and experience fewer interruptions. However, research that measures output directly gives a more mixed picture. In tasks that require deep concentration, such as writing code or analysing data, remote workers often perform as well as or better than their office-based colleagues. In contrast, roles that depend on frequent informal communication, including training new staff and developing early-stage ideas, appear to suffer when teams are rarely in the same place.

Many organisations have therefore adopted hybrid arrangements, in which employees spend two or three fixed days in the office. Supporters argue that this combines the focus of home working with the collaboration of the office. Critics point out that hybrid schedules only work if colleagues coordinate their office days; otherwise, employees may commute simply to join video calls from a different desk. The evidence so far suggests that the success of any arrangement depends less on location itself than on how deliberately managers organise the work.

explanation: B contradicts 'a more mixed picture'; E and F are not stated — the passage says success depends on how work is organised.

Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that around forty percent are endangered, meaning that they are no longer being learned by children as a first language. A language rarely disappears because its speakers suddenly abandon it. More often, the decline happens gradually over several generations. Parents who speak a minority language at home may decide that their children will have better economic prospects if they grow up speaking the dominant national language, and schools, media and employers frequently reinforce this choice.

The loss of a language involves more than the loss of words. Languages encode detailed knowledge about local plants, animals, landscapes and social relationships, much of which has never been written down. When the last fluent speakers die, this knowledge may disappear with them. For this reason, many communities have started revitalisation programmes, such as language nests in which young children are cared for entirely in the heritage language. The results vary, but several languages that were once spoken only by elderly people now have a new generation of young speakers.

Medieval mapmakers combined travellers' reports, ancient texts and religious beliefs, producing maps that tell us more about how their creators viewed the world than about its actual shape. Why do people continue to believe information that has been shown to be false? Psychologists have identified several reasons. One is the continued influence effect: even after a claim is corrected, people may still rely on the original information when reasoning about an event, especially if the correction does not offer an alternative explanation. Another factor is familiarity. Repeated exposure to a statement makes it feel more true, a phenomenon sometimes called the illusory truth effect.

People are also more likely to accept information that fits their existing beliefs and to question information that challenges them. This tendency, known as confirmation bias, can make corrections less effective when they come from sources people distrust.

Researchers have tested strategies to reduce the spread of misinformation. Warning people in advance about common manipulation techniques, sometimes called prebunking, appears to make them more resistant. Corrections are more effective when they explain why the false claim is wrong and provide a clear alternative account, rather than simply stating that it is untrue.

Traditional economic theory suggested that setting wages above the market level would reduce employment, as businesses would hire fewer workers. However, studies since the 1990s have complicated the picture. Fresh water covers only a tiny fraction of the Earth's surface, and much of it is locked in ice or underground. As populations grow and climates change, many regions face increasing water stress. Agriculture accounts for around seventy percent of global freshwater use, mainly for irrigation, so improving efficiency on farms is particularly important.

Drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots of plants through pipes, can reduce water use considerably compared with flooding fields. Sensors that measure soil moisture allow farmers to water crops only when needed. Choosing crops suited to local conditions can also make a large difference, as some crops require far more water than others.

Cities are also adopting new strategies, including fixing leaking pipes, which can waste a significant share of treated water, collecting rainwater and recycling wastewater for uses such as irrigation and industry. In some places, treated wastewater is even purified to drinking standard, although public acceptance of this approach varies.

options.text: Increasing the flooding of fields.
Fixing leaking pipes in cities.
Stopping all wastewater recycling.
Growing crops that need more water.
Drip irrigation.
Using soil moisture sensors.

Libraries have existed for thousands of years, but their role has changed dramatically. The ancient Library of Alexandria aimed to collect copies of every book in the known world, serving scholars rather than the general public. For much of history, access to books was limited to the wealthy, religious institutions and universities.

Public libraries funded by taxes became widespread in the nineteenth century, reflecting a belief that education should be available to everyone. Industrialists and philanthropists, such as Andrew Carnegie, funded thousands of library buildings in English-speaking countries. These libraries offered working people opportunities for self-education and became important community institutions.

In the digital age, some have predicted that libraries would become unnecessary. Instead, many have adapted, offering internet access, digital resources, children's activities and help with tasks such as job applications. For people without computers at home, libraries remain one of the few places where they can get online free of charge.

Many people assume that multitasking allows them to get more done. Research suggests otherwise. When we attempt two demanding tasks at once, such as writing an email while listening to a lecture, the brain must repeatedly switch attention between them. Each switch carries a small cost in time and accuracy, and these costs add up.

Studies of students show that those who frequently switch between studying and checking social media take longer to complete assignments and remember less of what they studied. Interestingly, people who multitask most often tend to overestimate their ability to do so and perform worse on tests of attention than those who multitask less.

Some activities can be combined successfully, particularly when one is automatic, such as walking while talking. The problem arises when both tasks require conscious thought. Experts recommend setting aside blocks of time for focused work, turning off notifications and grouping similar tasks together.

Tourism can bring significant economic benefits to developing regions, creating jobs and supporting local businesses. However, the benefits are not always distributed fairly. In some destinations, a large share of tourist spending goes to international hotel chains and tour companies, leaving relatively little for local communities.

Community-based tourism attempts to address this. In such projects, local people own and manage accommodation, guide visitors and decide how income is used, often investing in schools, health care or conservation. Visitors may stay in village homes, learn traditional skills and experience daily life in ways that conventional tourism rarely offers.

Community-based projects face challenges, including limited marketing budgets, difficulty reaching international customers and the risk that traditions become performances staged for tourists. Successful projects often partner with non-governmental organisations or responsible travel companies, which provide training and access to markets while leaving control with the community.

Volcanic eruptions are among the most dramatic natural events, but scientists have become increasingly skilled at monitoring active volcanoes. Before an eruption, magma moving beneath the surface often causes small earthquakes, changes in the shape of the ground and increases in gases such as sulphur dioxide. Instruments placed around volcanoes can detect these signs.

Satellites also play an important role, measuring tiny changes in ground height over large areas and detecting heat. By combining different types of data, scientists can sometimes warn authorities days or weeks in advance, allowing evacuations that save lives.

However, forecasting remains difficult. Some volcanoes show signs of unrest for years without erupting, while others erupt with little warning. False alarms can be costly and may reduce public trust in future warnings. Scientists therefore usually describe eruption risk in terms of probabilities rather than certainties, and work closely with local authorities to plan appropriate responses.

The history of chocolate stretches back thousands of years to Central America, where the Olmec, Maya and Aztec peoples used cacao beans to make a bitter drink, often flavoured with spices. Cacao was highly valued; the Aztecs even used the beans as a form of currency.

When Spanish explorers brought cacao to Europe in the sixteenth century, the drink was initially popular among the wealthy, who added sugar to suit European tastes. The industrial revolution transformed chocolate production. In the nineteenth century, new machines made it possible to press cocoa butter from the beans, leading to the creation of solid chocolate bars, and later to milk chocolate.

Today, chocolate is a global industry, but most cacao is grown by small farmers in West Africa, many of whom earn very low incomes. Concerns about poverty and child labour in cacao farming have led to certification schemes and initiatives aimed at improving conditions, although critics argue that progress has been slow.

Handwriting is taught less in many schools than it once was, as typing on keyboards and tablets has become the main way students produce written work. Some educators welcome this change, arguing that digital skills are more relevant to modern life and that typing allows students to write and edit more quickly.

However, a growing body of research suggests that handwriting may have benefits that typing does not. Studies have found that students who take lecture notes by hand often remember the material better than those who type, possibly because writing by hand is slower and forces them to summarise ideas in their own words rather than copying everything. Brain imaging research also indicates that forming letters by hand activates areas involved in reading and memory in young children.

Most researchers do not argue for abandoning keyboards. Instead, they suggest that schools should continue to teach handwriting in the early years and help older students choose the method that best suits each task.
